commands.name: grep
commands.summary: Search text using patterns — print lines matching a regex from files or stdin.
commands.explanation: grep filters lines matching a regular expression. -r scans directories recursively, -v inverts to show non-matching lines, -P enables Perl-compatible regex. Use --include to scope recursive searches to specific file types.

flags.desc: Print lines that do NOT match
Only print filenames with at least one match
Use Perl-compatible regex for advanced patterns
Scope recursive search to files matching a glob

examples.desc: Find ERROR lines with line numbers across all log files
Show nginx config without comment lines
Extract failed SSH login IPs using Perl regex

commands.pro_tip: Use `grep -c ''` to count total lines in a file — faster than `wc -l` when already in a grep pipeline.

commands.name: awk
commands.summary: Powerful text processing language for pattern scanning and field-based reporting.
commands.risk_reason: Read-only text transformation unless piped to write operations.
commands.explanation: awk processes text line-by-line, splitting each into fields ($1, $2, etc.) by a delimiter (default: whitespace). Supports conditionals, loops, and arithmetic — ideal for log analysis, report generation, and structured text extraction.

flags.desc: Set field separator (-F: for colon-delimited files like /etc/passwd)
Assign a variable before program execution
Read awk program from a file

examples.desc: Print first and last field from each line (e.g. IP and status code)
List all usernames with UID >= 1000 (regular users)
Count ERROR occurrences in a log file

commands.pro_tip: `awk 'NR==FNR{a[$0];next} $0 in a'` finds common lines between two files — a classic awk idiom for set intersection without sorting.

commands.name: sed
commands.summary: Stream editor — transform text using substitution, deletion, and insertion.
commands.risk_reason: In-place editing with -i permanently modifies files without undo.
cautions: `sed -i` edits files in place with no undo — use -i.bak.
Test the expression without -i first and diff the result.
GNU and BSD/macOS sed differ (macOS needs `-i ""`; -E vs \+ handling).
commands.explanation: sed reads input line by line applying editing commands. The `s/pattern/replacement/flags` command substitutes text. -i edits files in place. Always test with a dry run (without -i) before modifying files.

flags.desc: Edit file in-place (use -i.bak to keep a backup)
Suppress automatic printing of pattern space
Add a script command to execute

examples.desc: Replace hostname in config, keeping .bak backup
Print only lines 100 to 200 from a large log
Remove all blank lines from a file

commands.pro_tip: Always use `-i.bak` instead of bare `-i` — it creates a backup and is portable across Linux and macOS.

commands.name: sort
commands.summary: Sort lines of text — alphabetically, numerically, or by a specific field.
commands.risk_reason: Read-only by default; modifies files only when using -o.
commands.explanation: sort reads lines from files or stdin and outputs them sorted. -n sorts numerically, -r reverses, -k selects a key column, -u deduplicates. Combine with uniq and awk for powerful log analysis and data processing pipelines.

flags.desc: Sort by numeric value, not lexicographic order
Sort by a specific field/column (e.g. -k2 for 2nd field)
Output only unique lines, removing duplicates
Write result to a file (safe even if same as input)

examples.desc: Top 20 lines by 5th column descending — e.g. largest request sizes
List log directories sorted largest-first (human-readable sizes)
Sort /etc/passwd by UID (3rd colon-delimited field) numerically

commands.pro_tip: Use `sort -u` instead of `sort | uniq` — it deduplicates during the sort pass itself, which is faster on large inputs.

commands.name: diff
commands.summary: Compare files line by line and show differences.
commands.explanation: diff compares two files and outputs the differences in a format that can be applied as a patch. The -u flag produces unified diff format (the standard for patches and code review). Useful for config auditing, reviewing changes before applying, and generating patches.

examples.desc: Show changes since backup in patch format

examples.cmd: diff <(kubectl get cm myconfig -o yaml) config.yaml
examples.desc: Compare live ConfigMap with local file

commands.pro_tip: Use `diff <(command1) <(command2)` with process substitution to compare command outputs without creating temp files — works for comparing live config with desired state.

commands.name: wc
commands.summary: Count lines, words, characters, or bytes in files.
commands.explanation: wc (word count) counts newlines, words, characters, and bytes in files or stdin. Invaluable for quick data validation — checking how many records are in a file, confirming a log has expected line counts, or measuring output size.

examples.desc: Count YAML files in current directory

commands.pro_tip: Use `grep -c 'pattern' file` instead of `grep 'pattern' file | wc -l` — it's faster and more efficient for counting matching lines.

commands.name: cut
commands.summary: Extract specific fields or character ranges from text.
commands.explanation: cut extracts columns from text by delimiter (-d and -f) or character position (-c). A staple for parsing structured output like /etc/passwd, CSV files, or command output with consistent delimiters.

examples.desc: Extract first and third CSV columns
Show only first 10 characters per line

commands.pro_tip: For multi-character delimiters or more complex field logic, switch to `awk -F 'delim' '{print $2}'` — cut only supports single-character delimiters.

commands.name: tr
commands.summary: Translate, squeeze, or delete characters in text streams.
commands.risk_reason: Modifies stdout only; doesn't touch source files.
commands.explanation: tr translates or transforms characters — replacing, deleting, or squeezing repeated characters. Only works on stdin/stdout, not files directly. Frequently used for case conversion, removing unwanted characters, and cleaning data.

flags.desc: Use complement of the character set

commands.pro_tip: Use `tr -d '\r'` to fix Windows line endings in scripts cloned on Linux — a common cause of 'bad interpreter' errors.

commands.name: uniq
commands.summary: Filter or count adjacent duplicate lines in sorted input.
commands.risk_reason: Read-only unless redirected to overwrite source.
commands.explanation: uniq removes or counts duplicate lines, but only works on adjacent duplicates — always sort first. Combined with sort | uniq -c | sort -rn, it produces frequency counts of any text data.

examples.desc: Show IPs that appear more than once
Show lines that appear exactly once

commands.pro_tip: The pattern `sort | uniq -c | sort -rn` is one of the most powerful one-liners in DevOps — use it to analyze access logs, error frequencies, or any text data.

commands.name: head
commands.summary: Output the first N lines of a file.
commands.explanation: head outputs the first 10 lines by default (or N lines with -n). Essential for quickly previewing large files without loading them entirely. Also useful for extracting file headers in scripts.
commands.pro_tip: Use `head -n -5 file.txt` (negative N) to print everything except the last 5 lines — a lesser-known but powerful trick.

commands.name: tail
commands.summary: Output the last N lines of a file; follow live output.
commands.explanation: tail outputs the last N lines (default 10). The -f flag follows a file as it grows — the standard way to monitor live logs. -F is more robust than -f as it handles log rotation.

flags.desc: Follow file growth in real time

examples.desc: Stream and filter errors in real time
Skip header row (output from line 2 onward)

commands.pro_tip: Use `tail -F` instead of `tail -f` in production log monitoring — it reconnects when the file is rotated, preventing silent monitoring gaps.

commands.name: less
commands.summary: Page through file content interactively with search and navigation.
cautions: Inside less, `!command` runs a shell command and `v` opens an editor — beware of piping sensitive files on shared screens.
commands.explanation: less is an interactive file viewer that loads files page-by-page (unlike cat). Supports forward/backward navigation, regex search with /, and following live files with F. Handles arbitrarily large files efficiently.

flags.desc: Exit if content fits on screen

examples.desc: Open with line numbers, jump to first ERROR

commands.pro_tip: Inside less, press `F` to enter follow mode (like tail -f), then `Ctrl+C` to stop following and browse backward — the best of both worlds.

commands.name: tee
commands.summary: Write to stdout and one or more files simultaneously.
commands.risk_reason: Creates or overwrites files; use -a to append.
cautions: `tee file` truncates the file first — use -a to append.
With sudo: `cmd | sudo tee /etc/file` overwrites the whole file; back it up first.
commands.explanation: tee reads from stdin and writes to both stdout and specified files simultaneously — splitting the pipeline. Essential when you want to log output while still piping it to another command.

flags.desc: Append to files instead of overwriting

examples.cmd: kubectl get pods | tee pods.txt | grep Running
examples.desc: Save and filter in one step
Write to privileged file via sudo tee

commands.pro_tip: Use `sudo tee` instead of `sudo echo >` when writing to privileged files — `sudo echo >` doesn't work because redirection happens in the user shell, not as root.

commands.name: xargs
commands.summary: Build and execute commands from standard input.
commands.risk_reason: Can trigger bulk operations; test with -p or echo first.
cautions: Whitespace splitting breaks on filenames with spaces — use `find -print0 | xargs -0`.
Test with `echo` or -p before running destructive commands.
Without -r, GNU xargs runs the command once even when the input is empty.
commands.explanation: xargs reads items from stdin and passes them as arguments to a command. Handles the case where a command doesn't natively read from stdin. With -P, it runs multiple processes in parallel — a simple way to parallelize shell operations.

flags.desc: Replace placeholder string with each input item
Input items are null-terminated (safe for filenames with spaces)

examples.desc: Count lines in all log files

examples.cmd: cat pods.txt | xargs -I{} kubectl delete pod {}
examples.desc: Delete pods listed in a file

commands.pro_tip: Always use `find -print0 | xargs -0` when filenames might contain spaces or newlines — the default newline separator will cause silent failures.

commands.name: jq
commands.summary: Command-line JSON processor and transformer.
commands.risk_reason: Read-only unless redirected to overwrite a file.
commands.explanation: jq is a lightweight, flexible JSON processor. It slices, filters, transforms, and reformats JSON data with a pipeline syntax. Essential for working with API responses, Kubernetes output, and cloud CLI tools that return JSON.

flags.desc: Output raw strings without JSON quotes
Read all input into an array
Return exit code 1 if result is false/null

examples.desc: Filter active items from API response

commands.pro_tip: Use `jq -e 'expression' && echo ok || echo fail` in CI scripts — jq exits non-zero if the result is null/false, making it a powerful JSON-aware conditional.

commands.name: yq
commands.summary: Command-line YAML/JSON/XML processor (like jq but for YAML).
commands.risk_reason: Read-only unless -i flag is used (in-place edit).
cautions: `yq -i` edits files in place — keep a backup or use version control.
Different yq implementations (mikefarah vs python-yq) have different syntax.
commands.explanation: yq processes YAML, JSON, XML, and TOML files with a jq-compatible syntax. Invaluable for editing Kubernetes manifests, Helm values files, and CI config files without breaking structure. The -i flag edits files in-place.

examples.desc: Read replica count from a manifest
Convert YAML to JSON for jq processing

examples.cmd: yq eval-all '. as $item ireduce ({}; . * $item)' base.yaml override.yaml

commands.pro_tip: Use yq to patch image tags in manifests during CI: `yq -i '.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image = "app:v1.2.3"' deploy.yaml` — cleaner than sed on YAML.

commands.name: base64
commands.summary: Encode or decode data using Base64.
commands.risk_reason: Encoding is not encryption — don't use for secrets.
cautions: Base64 is encoding, not encryption — never treat it as protecting secrets.
commands.explanation: base64 encodes binary data as printable ASCII text, or decodes it back. Used in Kubernetes secrets, JWT tokens, basic auth headers, and embedding binary data in text formats. Note: base64 is encoding, not encryption — encoded data is trivially reversible.

flags.desc: Wrap encoded lines at N characters (0 to disable)

examples.cmd: kubectl get secret mysecret -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d

examples.desc: Base64 encode certificate without line wraps

commands.pro_tip: Use `echo -n` (no newline) before piping to base64 — without -n, the newline character is included in the encoding and your decoded value will have a trailing newline.

commands.name: column
commands.summary: Format text into aligned columns for readable tabular output.
commands.explanation: column formats text into evenly-spaced columns, making tabular data human-readable. The -t flag auto-detects and aligns fields. Transforms messy whitespace-separated output into a table without writing awk.

examples.desc: Format mount output as aligned table

commands.pro_tip: Pipe any space-separated output through `column -t` for instant readability — especially useful for custom monitoring scripts that emit structured data.

commands.name: printf
commands.summary: Format and print data with precise control over output format.
commands.explanation: printf formats output using format specifiers (like C printf). More predictable than echo — doesn't add a newline by default, handles escape sequences consistently, and supports format strings for aligned output in scripts.
commands.pro_tip: Use printf instead of echo in scripts for portability — echo behavior with -e and escape sequences varies across shells and implementations.

commands.name: patch
commands.summary: Apply a diff/patch file to update source files.
commands.risk_reason: Modifies files; backup before applying unknown patches.
cautions: Back up first (-b) or run --dry-run to check the patch applies cleanly.
Patches from untrusted sources can modify any file under the target directory.
The wrong -p strip level patches the wrong files.
commands.explanation: patch applies changes described in a diff file to the original files. The standard workflow is: generate a patch with diff -u, review it, then apply with patch. Used for distributing fixes without sending full files.

flags.desc: Strip N leading path components from filenames
Reverse: undo a previously applied patch
Preview what patch would do without applying

examples.desc: Apply patch (strip 1 path component, standard for git patches)

examples.cmd: git diff HEAD~1 HEAD > change.patch && patch -p1 < change.patch
examples.desc: Backport a git commit as a patch

commands.pro_tip: Always use `patch --dry-run` first to verify a patch applies cleanly before committing — especially critical for patches from external sources against your specific version.

commands.name: strings
commands.summary: Extract printable strings from binary files.
commands.explanation: strings extracts sequences of printable characters from binary files — useful for quickly inspecting executables for embedded configuration, version strings, URLs, credentials, or other readable content without a full reverse engineering setup.

flags.desc: Scan entire file (not just data sections)

examples.desc: Find version string in curl binary

commands.pro_tip: Use `strings -n 8 binary | grep -E '^[a-zA-Z]{8,}$'` to filter out noise — longer minimum length and letter-only filter finds meaningful text like hostnames and keys.

commands.name: xxd
commands.summary: Create or reverse a hex dump of binary data.
commands.explanation: xxd creates hex dumps of files showing both hex values and ASCII representation, and can reverse hex back to binary. Used for inspecting binary file formats, debugging network protocols, and examining any file at the byte level.

flags.desc: Reverse: convert hex dump back to binary

examples.desc: View first few bytes of a binary (check magic bytes)
Convert hex dump back to binary

commands.pro_tip: Use `xxd -l 4 file` to read just the first 4 bytes (magic number) — fast file type verification at the byte level. ELF binaries start with 7f454c46, PNG with 89504e47.

commands.name: awk advanced
commands.summary: Advanced awk: multi-condition processing, BEGIN/END blocks, associative arrays.
commands.explanation: awk is a full programming language embedded in the shell pipeline. Beyond simple field printing, it supports BEGIN/END blocks for pre/post processing, associative arrays for aggregation, conditional logic, and arithmetic — replacing Python for many data processing tasks.

examples.desc: Sum a column across all lines

examples.cmd: awk '{count[$9]++} END{for(code in count) print code, count[code]}' access.log | sort -k2 -rn
examples.desc: Count HTTP status codes in access log

commands.pro_tip: Use `awk '{count[$1]++} END{for(k in count) print count[k], k}' | sort -rn` for instant frequency analysis of any column — replaces sort|uniq -c for multi-field grouping.

commands.name: sed advanced
commands.summary: Advanced sed: multi-line editing, in-place replacement, complex patterns.
commands.risk_reason: In-place editing (-i) modifies files; backup with -i.bak first.
cautions: -i modifies files in place — use -i.bak.
Complex multi-line scripts are hard to review; keep them in a file (-f script.sed).
Test on a copy of the file first.
commands.explanation: Beyond simple substitution, sed supports in-place file editing, multi-line patterns, address ranges, and script files. The -i flag is essential for automated config management — patching configuration files without opening an editor.
commands.pro_tip: Always use `-i.bak` in scripts for in-place edits — creates a backup automatically. Remove backup files with `find . -name '*.bak' -delete` after confirming changes.

commands.name: grep advanced
commands.summary: Advanced grep: recursive search, context, PCRE patterns, and file filtering.
commands.explanation: Beyond basic pattern matching, grep supports recursive directory search, context lines around matches, Perl-compatible regex (PCRE), and filtering by file type. Used heavily for log analysis, code search, and configuration auditing.

examples.desc: Find password references in all config files
Show 5 lines after and 2 before each CRITICAL match
Find config files that DON'T have strict_mode

commands.pro_tip: Use `grep -rn 'pattern' . --include='*.py' --exclude-dir='.git'` for code search — the include/exclude flags prevent searching binaries and version control directories.

commands.name: echo
commands.summary: Print text
commands.risk_reason: Prints text; can expose secrets if variables are expanded into logs.
cautions: `echo $SECRET` in CI logs or shared terminals leaks the secret.
`> file` truncates the target; use >> to append.
commands.explanation: Writes its arguments to standard output. Behavior of -e/-n differs between shells; printf is more portable.

flags.desc: Do not print the trailing newline

examples.desc: Append a line to a file

commands.name: nl
commands.summary: Number lines
commands.explanation: Prints a file with line numbers (only for non-empty lines by default).

commands.name: paste
commands.summary: Merge lines of files side by side
commands.explanation: Joins corresponding lines of files using a delimiter (default tab).

flags.desc: Serial: join all lines of one file

commands.name: join
commands.summary: Join lines of two sorted files on a field
commands.risk_reason: Read-only; unsorted input yields wrong results.
commands.explanation: Relational join of two files on a common field. Inputs must be sorted on the join field.

examples.desc: Join CSV files on the first field

commands.name: comm
commands.summary: Compare two sorted files line by line
commands.explanation: Shows lines unique to each file and lines common to both.

examples.desc: Lines in a but not in b

commands.name: tac
commands.summary: Print file lines in reverse
commands.explanation: Like cat, but prints the last line first.

commands.name: rev
commands.summary: Reverse characters in each line
commands.explanation: Reverses each line character by character.

commands.name: fold
commands.summary: Wrap long lines
commands.explanation: Wraps input lines to a given width. See the flags and examples below, and run `man fold` for the full reference.

commands.name: fmt
commands.summary: Reformat paragraphs
commands.explanation: Reflows text to a target width. See the flags and examples below, and run `man fmt` for the full reference.

commands.name: expand
commands.summary: Convert tabs to spaces
commands.risk_reason: Read-only unless redirected over the source.
cautions: `expand f > f` truncates the file before reading it — write to a new file.
commands.explanation: Replaces tabs with spaces. See the flags and examples below, and run `man expand` for the full reference.

commands.name: iconv
commands.summary: Convert text encodings
commands.risk_reason: Output can silently lose characters if the target encoding cannot represent them.
cautions: -c silently discards unconvertible characters.
Write to a new file; do not redirect onto the input.
commands.explanation: Converts between character encodings such as ISO-8859-1 and UTF-8.

flags.desc: Drop characters that cannot be converted

commands.name: dos2unix
commands.summary: Convert Windows line endings
cautions: Modifies files in place — use -n or keep a copy under version control.
Running it on binary files corrupts them (the tool normally skips them).
commands.explanation: Converts CRLF to LF (and unix2dos does the reverse). Fixes “bad interpreter: ^M” errors in scripts.

commands.name: zless
commands.summary: View compressed files
commands.explanation: Pager for gzip-compressed files. See the flags and examples below, and run `man zless` for the full reference.

commands.name: egrep
commands.summary: Extended grep
commands.explanation: Equivalent to grep -E; deprecated spelling in favour of grep -E.

commands.name: rg
commands.summary: ripgrep: fast recursive search
commands.risk_reason: Read-only; respects .gitignore and skips hidden files by default so results may look incomplete.
cautions: Ignored/hidden files are skipped — use --hidden or -uu if a match is missing.
commands.explanation: A fast grep replacement that searches recursively, with sensible defaults.

commands.name: fd
commands.summary: Fast, friendly find alternative
commands.risk_reason: Read-only; skips hidden/ignored files by default.
cautions: -x runs a command per match — preview with `fd -e tmp` before adding `-x rm`.
commands.explanation: Simpler syntax than find with colored output and .gitignore awareness.

commands.name: bat
commands.summary: cat with syntax highlighting
commands.explanation: A cat clone with syntax highlighting, line numbers and git integration (batcat on Debian).

commands.name: shuf
commands.summary: Shuffle or pick random lines
commands.explanation: Randomly permutes input lines or picks N of them.

flags.desc: Pick random numbers from a range

commands.name: seq
commands.summary: Print a sequence of numbers
commands.explanation: Generates numeric sequences for loops and tests.

commands.name: envsubst
commands.summary: Substitute environment variables in text
commands.risk_reason: Can expand secrets into output files and logs.
cautions: Unlisted variables become empty strings silently — restrict substitution to a variable list.
Rendered files may contain secrets; protect their permissions.
commands.explanation: Replaces $VAR placeholders in a template with environment values — common in config rendering.

commands.name: xmllint
commands.summary: Parse and validate XML
commands.explanation: Formats, validates and queries XML with XPath.

commands.name: csvkit
commands.summary: CSV tools suite
commands.explanation: A set of command-line CSV tools: csvcut, csvgrep, csvstat, csvsql, in2csv.

commands.name: ed
commands.summary: Line editor
cautions: Edits in place with no backup — copy the file first.
commands.explanation: Classic line editor; useful in scripts for in-place edits. `ed` commands are read from stdin.

commands.name: vim
commands.summary: Vi IMproved text editor
commands.risk_reason: Edits files directly; swap/undo files can store sensitive data.
cautions: Use `sudoedit` instead of `sudo vim` so plugins and your config do not run as root.
Swap, backup and viminfo files can contain secrets — use `vim -n` or `set noswapfile` for sensitive files.
Editing live config directly can break services: test (nginx -t, visudo -c) before reloading.
commands.explanation: Modal text editor. Esc to command mode, :wq to save and quit, :q! to quit without saving.

examples.desc: Edit a file (use sudoedit for root files)

commands.name: nano
commands.summary: Simple terminal text editor
commands.risk_reason: Edits files directly; mistakes in system configs can break services.
cautions: Wrapped lines in config files like fstab or sshd_config can silently break them — use -w.
Validate config syntax before reloading services.
commands.explanation: Beginner-friendly editor. Ctrl+O writes, Ctrl+X exits, Ctrl+W searches.

flags.desc: Disable line wrapping (important for config files)

commands.name: od
commands.summary: Dump bytes in octal/other formats
commands.explanation: Octal dump of files. See the flags and examples below, and run `man od` for the full reference.

commands.name: hexdump
commands.summary: Hex dump
commands.explanation: Displays files in hex and ASCII. See the flags and examples below, and run `man hexdump` for the full reference.

commands.name: cksum
commands.summary: CRC checksum
commands.explanation: POSIX CRC; not cryptographic. See the flags and examples below, and run `man cksum` for the full reference.

commands.name: pr
commands.summary: Paginate text for printing
commands.explanation: Formats text into pages/columns. See the flags and examples below, and run `man pr` for the full reference.

commands.name: tsort
commands.summary: Topological sort
commands.explanation: Sorts dependency pairs. See the flags and examples below, and run `man tsort` for the full reference.

commands.name: look
commands.summary: Find lines starting with a prefix
commands.explanation: Binary search in sorted files/dictionary.

commands.name: sponge
commands.summary: Soak up input before writing a file
cautions: Overwrites the file at the end — keep a backup.
commands.explanation: From moreutils: lets you modify a file in a pipeline.

commands.name: gawk
commands.summary: GNU awk
cautions: -i inplace overwrites the file; use `INPLACE_SUFFIX`.
commands.explanation: Extended awk with -i inplace option. See the flags and examples below, and run `man gawk` for the full reference.
